items.body:
BERLIN. **Verdreckte Toiletten, fehlende Privatsphäre, unangenehme Gerüche: Was für viele Schülerinnen und Schüler zum Alltag gehört, hat Folgen, die weit über den Zustand der sanitären Anlagen hinausgehen. Manche Kinder und Jugendliche vermeiden es sogar, während des Schultags zu trinken, um nicht auf die Toilette gehen zu müssen. Dabei können Schulen durchaus etwas verändern – und die Betroffenen selbst spielen dabei eine entscheidende Rolle. Wie das gelingen kann, zeigt eine kostenlose Online-Veranstaltung der Heinz Trox-Stiftung am 25. November, die News4teachers als Medienpartner unterstützt.**

Die Toilette gehört zu den wenigen Orten in einer Schule, an denen Schülerinnen und Schüler für einen Moment unbeobachtet sein können. Eigentlich. Denn vielerorts sind die sanitären Anlagen in einem Zustand, der Kinder und Jugendliche eher abschreckt, als ihnen einen geschützten Raum zu bieten. Verschmutzungen, beschädigte Einrichtungen und fehlende Rückzugsmöglichkeiten können dazu führen, dass Schülerinnen und Schüler den Toilettengang möglichst lange hinauszögern.

Wie weitreichend die Folgen sein können, verdeutlicht eine Untersuchung der German Toilet Organization (GTO) und der Universität Bonn, deren Ergebnisse 2023 veröffentlicht wurden. Befragt wurden 949 Neuntklässlerinnen und Neuntklässler an 17 weiterführenden Schulen in Berlin. Sie bewerteten ihre Schultoiletten durchschnittlich mit der Schulnote 4 minus. 46 Prozent gaben an, das Wasserlassen in der Schule zu vermeiden, beim Stuhlgang waren es sogar 85 Prozent. Mehr als ein Viertel der Befragten berichtete, deshalb oft oder immer weniger zu essen oder zu trinken.

Damit wird aus einem vermeintlichen Problem der Gebäudeunterhaltung eine Frage der Gesundheit und des Wohlbefindens. Doch wer kann daran etwas ändern? Und wie lassen sich Schülerinnen und Schüler an Verbesserungen beteiligen, statt lediglich neue Verhaltensregeln für die Toilettennutzung aufzustellen?

Diesen Fragen widmet sich die zweite Ausgabe des digitalen Gesprächsformats „ZUKUNFTSRAUM SCHULE LIVE“ der Heinz Trox-Stiftung. Unter dem Titel „Raus aus der Schmuddelecke: Schultoiletten als erweiterter Lehrraum“ diskutieren am Mittwoch, 25. November 2026, von 16 bis 17 Uhr Thilo Panzerbieter, Gründer und Geschäftsführer der German Toilet Organization, und Lilian Ruß, Leiterin der Initiative „Toiletten machen Schule“.

## „Schüler*innen kennen ihre Schultoiletten meist am besten. Sie nutzen sie jeden Tag, haben aber selten etwas mit Ausstattung und Instandhaltung zu tun“

Im Mittelpunkt steht ein Ansatz, der über die Sanierung beschädigter Toiletten hinausgeht: Schülerinnen und Schüler sollen selbst daran mitwirken, die Situation zu erfassen, Probleme zu benennen und Lösungen zu entwickeln. Aus einem Ort, der im Schulalltag häufig Anlass für Beschwerden ist, kann so ein Raum werden, in dem Beteiligung und Verantwortung praktisch erfahrbar werden.

„Schüler*innen kennen ihre Schultoiletten meist am besten. Sie nutzen sie jeden Tag, haben aber selten etwas mit Ausstattung und Instandhaltung zu tun. Wenn wir ihre Perspektive einbeziehen und sie selbst entscheiden, was mit diesem Raum passiert und wie er aussieht, wächst auch ihr Verantwortungsbewusstsein. Und sie erfahren an diesem stillen Ort ganz konkret, was Teilhabe und Selbstwirksamkeit bedeuten“, sagt Lilian Ruß.

Die Initiative „Toiletten machen Schule“ unterstützt Schulen dabei, einen solchen Prozess selbst zu organisieren. Ein kostenfreies Hilfsportal stellt dafür Umfragetools, Checklisten, Beteiligungsmethoden und Praxisbeispiele bereit. Schulen können zunächst ein Toilettenteam gründen, anschließend gemeinsam mit den Schülerinnen und Schülern den Zustand der Anlagen untersuchen und schließlich Maßnahmen entwickeln und priorisieren.

Dabei geht es nicht allein um die Gestaltung der Räume. Auch Fragen der Reinigung, der Instandhaltung und des Umgangs miteinander müssen geklärt werden. Für nachhaltige Verbesserungen ist deshalb die Zusammenarbeit verschiedener Beteiligter wichtig: Schülerinnen und Schüler, Lehrkräfte, Schulleitungen, Eltern, Hausmeisterei, Reinigungspersonal und Schulträger müssen gemeinsam Lösungen finden.

Allerdings können Schulen nicht sämtliche Probleme in Eigenregie beheben. Die regelmäßige Reinigung, die Instandhaltung der Anlagen und die Beseitigung baulicher Schäden liegen wesentlich in der Verantwortung der zuständigen Schulträger und Dienstleister. Beteiligungsprojekte können dazu beitragen, Missstände sichtbar zu machen, Prioritäten zu setzen und den Umgang mit den Räumen zu verändern. Sie ersetzen aber nicht die notwendigen Investitionen und organisatorischen Maßnahmen.

Für die Heinz Trox-Stiftung ist die Beschäftigung mit Schultoiletten Teil einer umfassenderen Frage: Welche räumlichen Bedingungen brauchen Kinder und Jugendliche, um sich in der Schule wohlzufühlen und gut lernen zu können?

Mit ihrem Projekt „Zukunftsraum Schule“ beschäftigt sich die Stiftung insbesondere mit Temperatur, Akustik, Innenraumluft und Licht. Diese vier Faktoren werden im sogenannten TAIL-Ansatz gemeinsam betrachtet. Die Qualität schulischer Räume soll dabei nicht nur anhand einzelner technischer Merkmale bewertet werden, sondern in ihrem Zusammenspiel.

Auch die Schultoiletten gehören aus Sicht der Stiftung zu einer solchen Betrachtung. Schließlich verbringen Schülerinnen und Schüler ihren Tag nicht ausschließlich im Klassenzimmer. Flure, Aufenthaltsbereiche, Pausenräume und sanitäre Anlagen prägen ebenfalls ihre Erfahrungen mit Schule.

„Mit Zukunftsraum Schule setzen wir uns für Räume ein, in denen Kinder gut lernen und sich wohlfühlen können. Das endet nicht an der Klassenzimmertür. Wer über Luft, Licht, Temperatur und Akustik spricht, muss auch die Orte mitdenken, die Kinder jeden Tag nutzen und oft meiden. Die Schultoilette zeigt zudem, wie viel sich bewegt, wenn Schüler*innen ihre Räume selbst bewerten und mitgestalten“, erklärt Christine Roßkothen, Vorstand der Heinz Trox-Stiftung.

## Why you should be reading Helen Garner (and where to start).

Last week, The Paris Review announced the winners of its annual literary awards. In 2027, Australian author Helen Garner will be feted with the Hadada, a prize that recognizes a writer’s lifelong literary contributions. I am here as an independent body to hype this choice.

Garner—a novelist, journalist, and diarist—writes big-hearted heroines who are often on the edge of a crisis. Her other fans include Lauren Groff, Lily King, Rumaan Alam, and Ben Lerner, but we are legion. Why, you ask?

In a recent piece for The Guardian , Emma Brockes also praised Garner’s “ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth.” And it’s true—that earthiness is what makes her work indelible. But it’s also just the tip of an iceberg.

Here are three of Garner’s best known books (and why you should make like the Parisians and pick them up, stat).

Monkey Grip , Garner’s 1977 debut, sent a shockwave through Australia. This novel chronicles a woman’s doomed-from-the-jump situationship with a heroin addict who charms her intermittently as they orbit a communal living situation.

A little like Susie Boyt’s sleeper hit, Loved and Missed , this book beautifully captures the recurring heartbreak involved in loving an addict. But it’s never saccharine, or sanctimonious.

Following a bohemian Melbourne milieu that echoes the author’s own set at the time, Garner’s non-judgmental portrait of freewheeling radicals brought out the moralizers on publication. Nora, our heroine, ruffled feathers for depicting ambivalent parenthood administered with a very loose latchkey. All adults in this book are libidinally motivated. Drugs and sex are world-structuring forces.

But what’s most exciting is how naked the prose is about all of that want. In Garner’s matter-of-fact voice, Nora’s thirst for the grifting Javo is rendered tender, abject, holy, and pathetic by turns. She feels like a real and vulnerable person with a mighty human flaw. The best kind of protagonist.

My favorite of Garner’s novels is The Children’s Bach . Another tale of domestic upheaval ignited by a charismatic chaos agent, this book traces the happily partnered Athena Fox’s infatuation with a blast from the past. Against reason, she leaves her partner and two small children for… a rock star.

What follows is a little predictable, but as with Monkey Grip the pleasure is in experiencing that slow road to ruin. (Or is it ecstasy?)

The third person POV serves this book, which manages to texturize everyone affected by Athena’s choices. She feels like a modern Nora, in the Ibsen sense.

The Spare Room is a cool, slim, spiky book. I find this Garner still gnaws at me. Following two semi-estranged old friends who fall back together when one seeks harbor following a terminal diagnosis, this novel depicts the unpleasant side of caretaking and the indignity of illness.

This book asks some truly itchy questions. Such as, what do you do when your patient is delusional—and/or, you want them out of your house?

As in the other novels, our protagonist chafes against conventionality and obligatory mutual obligation. And her extreme honesty hits you like a glass of cold water. As always, there’s a nakedness to a Garner subject. She doesn’t flinch from depicting those ugly emotions or unwanted thoughts.

In a review for the Times , Daphne Merkin once compared Garner to other “laconic and wayward,” ladies who specialize in the “art of artlessness, like Jean Rhys, Jane Bowles and Paula Fox.”

I agree with wayward, but I think that artful eye is in a class all its own. Do yourself a favor and join the Helen hive. Today.

### Brittany Allen

Brittany K. Allen is a writer and actor living in Brooklyn.

items.body:
Wissenschaftskommunikation ist politischer geworden und muss sich in einer zunehmend polarisierten Welt behaupten. Annette Leßmöllmann und Markus Weißkopf sprechen zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de über Erfolge, Herausforderungen und notwendigen Wandel.

Am 24. November 2016 ging Wissenschaftskommunikation.de online. In unserem [Schwerpunkt zum zehnjährigen Jubiläum](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wo-steht-die-wisskomm/)blicken wir auf prägende Entwicklungen zurück *und fragen, wo die Wissenschaftskommunikation heute steht.*

**Mit welcher Idee und welchem persönlichen Anspruch seid Ihr 2016 an der Gründung von Wissenschaftskommunikation.de beteiligt gewesen?**

**Markus Weißkopf** ist Redakteur des Research.Table bei Table.Media. Er war Geschäftsführer von Wissenschaft im Dialog und hat dort unter anderem die Plattform Wissenschaftskommunikation.de aufgebaut. Foto: WiD

Markus Weißkopf: Kurz zuvor hatten Wissenschaft im Dialog und der Bundesverband Hochschulkommunikation gemeinsam die [Leitlinien zur guten Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/leitlinien-zur-guten-wissenschaftskommunikation-85129/) veröffentlicht. In dem Zuge hatte die Community viel über gemeinsame Werte, aber auch über die Professionalisierung der Wissenschaftskommunikation diskutiert. Wissenschaftskommunikation.de sollte unter anderem eine Plattform für diese Themen bieten.

Annette Leßmöllmann: Die Plattform sollte zeigen: Wissenschaftskommunikation bedeutet mehr als nur Pressemitteilungen und Hochglanzmagazine. Mir war es ein Anliegen, Forschung und Praxis zusammenzubringen und somit die [Vermittlung der Wissenschaftskommunikationsforschung](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/kategorie/forschung/) voranzutreiben. Zum einen, um praxisrelevante Ergebnisse bekannt zu machen, zum anderen, um die theoretische Weiterentwicklung, die Interdisziplinarität und die Selbstreflexion des Forschungsfeldes zu zeigen. Gleichzeitig sollten Praxisfragen für die Forschung nachvollziehbar werden, um neue Forschung anzustoßen.

**Annette Leßmöllmann** (@annetteless.bsky.social) ist promovierte Linguistin und hat am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* den Lehrstuhl für Wissenschaftskommunikation mit dem Schwerpunkt Linguistik inne. Sie lehrt in den Bachelor- und Master-Studiengängen „Wissenschaft – Medien – Kommunikation“ (@WMKstudium).

**Welche Fragen oder Konfliktlinien aus der Gründungszeit beschäftigen die Community bis heute?**

Weißkopf: „Als Anlaufstelle Nr. 1 hat sich das Online-Lexikon Wikipedia im Internet längst etabliert. Die Wissenschaft sollte das Potenzial von Wikipedia für die Vermittlung fundierten Wissens ernsthaft prüfen.“ Das hat eine Pressesprecherin [im Rahmen des ersten Schwerpunkts „Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation“](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/blick-nach-vorn-wie-sieht-die-wissenschaftskommunikation-der-zukunft-aus-5-13517/) geschrieben. Natürlich ist das Prüfen wissenschaftsimmanent. Aber im Bereich der Kommunikation können wir es uns nicht erlauben, jahrelang zu prüfen. Die Wissenschaft hat nun ein Engagement bei oder für [Wikipedia](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/format/wikipedia/) so lange geprüft, bis es zu spät war. Nur einzelne Einrichtungen wie die Universität Innsbruck bilden hier Ausnahmen. Da würde ich mir manchmal mehr Mut zum Experimentieren wünschen!

Leßmöllmann: Was sich bereits vor zehn Jahren angekündigt hat: Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden. Dass sie in Interessenslagen und Machtstrukturen eingebettet ist und dass es als machtvoller kommunikativer Akt angesehen wird, wenn jemand „bestimmt“, was wahr oder falsch ist – das war damals eher ein Gedankenexperiment, ist heute aber deutlich als Konflikt zu spüren.

Es wird für die Wissenschaftskommunikation viel schwieriger, wenn es den Entscheider*innen reicht, dass sich etwas wahr anfühlt, auch wenn es nicht wahr ist. Dass etwa politische und gesellschaftliche Entscheidungen gegen den vorherrschenden wissenschaftlichen Konsens getroffen werden, ist angesichts der Klimakrise deutlich bedrohlicher und krisenhafter spürbar als noch vor zehn Jahren.

### „Wissenschaftskommunikation muss sich für Wissenschaftsfreiheit einsetzen und ist – teilweise notgedrungen – wesentlich politischer geworden.“

Annette Leßmöllmann

**Direkt mit dem ersten Schwerpunkt des Portals haben wir damals auf die** **[Zukunft der Wissenschaftskommunikation](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/zukunft-der-wissenschaftskommunikation/)** **geblickt. Welche damaligen Hoffnungen und Befürchtungen haben sich aus Eurer Sicht bewahrheitet und welche nicht?**

Leßmöllmann: Es hat sich die Hoffnung bewahrheitet, dass heute stärker darauf geachtet wird, Kommunikationsaktivitäten wissenschaftlich fundiert zu evaluieren. Zudem hat es funktioniert, dass sich die Community intensiver vernetzt und dass Forschung und Praxis enger zusammenarbeiten.

Es gab auch den Wunsch, dass Wissenschaftskommunikation stärker Teil der Gesellschaft und des täglichen Austauschs über die relevanten Themen der Zeit wird. In einem Aspekt hat sich der Wunsch bewahrheitet, allerdings anders als gedacht: Durch [generative Künstliche Intelligenz](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/themen/kuenstliche-intelligenz/) sind Wissen und Wissenschaft jetzt noch einfacher und dialogischer zu erreichen.

Gleichzeitig wurde die DIN-Norm der Kommunikation aufgeweicht: Es ist nicht mehr sicher, ob das Kommunizierte auch stimmt. Dies trägt zu einer Wissenskrise bei. Etwas dystopisch und pointiert formuliert: Gesagt und geglaubt wird, was gut klingt und auf die Interessen der eigenen Peer Group einzahlt. Das zeigt, dass wir in einer völlig anderen Welt als vor zehn Jahren leben. Die Rolle des Wissens, die demokratische Verankerung und die Wissenschaftsfreiheit stehen zur Debatte.

## Bickering Buildings A Dialogue Between the Churches of Athens in 1854

The churches of Athens had much to say in 1854, when an anonymous author staged a squabble between them in newsprint. Nikos Magouliotis eavesdrops on this chatter, finding personified anxieties about Greek architectural identity, foreign influence, and the newly formed nation’s relation to its past.

Published

November 24, 2026

Gabriel de Rumine’s 1858 photograph of Athens from the Acropolis. The Metropolitan Cathedral is under construction in the foreground — Source .

Buildings are often thought of as “silent witnesses of history”, but they have a history of talking, especially in moments of crisis. In a pamphlet published in London in 1641, at the height of the Reformation, two monuments that served as sites of Catholic devotion literally converse, trying to make sense of (and poke fun at) the Protestant vandalism against them. 1 In the eighteenth century, a whole genre of texts developed in which authors imagined what buildings might have said if they could speak to each other or passersby. 2

This was not just a matter for the popular press. The end of the eighteenth century saw the emergence of “architecture parlante” (speaking architecture), through a group of architects who argued that buildings ought to communicate their function and meaning to people, through figurative symbols, letters, or inscriptions. 3 When opinions about a certain monument or a cityscape predominate, buildings must speak for themselves to set things straight. This happened through experimental designs by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux and others, but also through pamphlets, broadsheets, cartoons, and newspaper articles that were written for a broader public and gave voice to the built environment. 4

In mid-nineteenth-century Athens, the furious construction of the new capital in the recently established Greek state produced a lot of new buildings, but little architectural theory. Academically trained architects in Athens may have been too busy designing, or too antagonistic and secretive, to share their theories in writing. But architectural criticism abounded in the popular press, often penned by anonymous authors and frequently satirical. On February 3, 1854, the Athenian newspaper Athena (Αθηνά) published an anonymous satirical text titled “A Dialogue between the Belfries of the Capital [Διάλογος των κωδωνοστασίων της Πρωτευούσης]”. 5 In it, the belfries of Athens’ churches debate current affairs and the future of the city, acutely aware of the shifting geopolitics of Europe.

Athens had become the Greek capital two decades earlier, and was the epicentre of intensive building activity. Plans were drawn up to rebuild it on a rectangular grid and expand it on monumental axes. 6 Its ancient sites were cleared of rubble and anything else that was seen as an obstruction, including Byzantine and Ottoman remains. 7 Monumental neoclassical buildings were erected to house the country’s new institutions: a university, an academy, a library, a palace . . . The small Ottoman town of Athens was trying to transform itself into a European capital.

Theophil Hansen’s 1859 watercolour plan for The Athenian Trilogy on Panepistimiou Avenue. Hansen was commissioned by King Otto to design the National Library of Greece (left), University of Athens (centre), and Academy of Athens (right). The buildings were completed, respectively, in 1903, 1864, and 1887 — Source .

Given this aspiration, it is fitting that the “Dialogue” opens with the belfry of the Byzantine church of Taxiarchs, a modest eleventh-century chapel that stood next to the Roman Agora and would in later years be demolished, 8 boasting with great confidence:

> All the travellers that pass by here fix their eyes on me and admire me. Many say that, in the whole world, there are only three belfries worth talking about: the one of [Our Lady of] Tinos, the one of [the Cathedral of] Strasbourg, and me . . . . And I do not say this out of any vanity — the other day I saw an [English] lord who not only observed me with great curiosity, but also cried in admiration: “By Zeus! This belfry is worthy of being transported to the British Museum!” . . . What other building has ever heard such praise from the Enlightened world? 9

In reality, few foreign travellers (whether onlookers or looters) or local authorities were interested in Greece’s Byzantine churches at that time. 10 Systematic efforts for their protection would begin toward the end of the nineteenth century, 11 but initially, these buildings received little attention, 12 despite the ostensible existence of a law ordering the preservation of the Byzantine, Venetian, and Turkish “relics of the Middle Ages”. 13 Many of these churches were left in disrepair or demolished to make way for new streets and buildings, 14 or even reclaimed as material for the construction of new churches. 15 A survey of Athens in 1833 documented a total of 115 churches, of which only 30 were deemed in a good enough condition to merit repairs; a survey made roughly a decade later indicated that only half of those survived. 16

Pierre Peytier’s drawing of the Fethiye Mosque and the Church of the Taxiarchs in Athens, ca. 1830s — Source .

André Couchaud’s architectural drawings of the Church of the Taxiarchs, from Choix d’églises bysantines en Grèce (1842) — Source .

items.body:
In a Buddhist temple in the northeast of Thailand, not far from the border with Laos, one can find the World's Only Dinosaur Pulpit.

Located in the city of Khon Kean, the fourth-largest city in Thailand and the heart of the Isan region, the pulpit can be found inside the Buddhist temple Wat That Phra Aram Luang. If you look closely, you'll notice there are dinosaur mural paintings on the walls inside the temple as well.

Having been the site of Thailand’s first dinosaur fossil discovery, Khon Kean boasts a variety of dinosaur-related sites. Dinosaur imagery is scattered throughout the entire region, giving a nod to this history. Among these references is the World's Only Dinosaur pulpit. The pulpit is shaped like a giant Phuwiangosaurus, Thailand’s native sauropod dinosaur. The dinosaur was originally discovered in the hills of Phu Wiang outside the city, and officially named in 1994 in honor of Her Royal Highness Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn.

Monks reportedly stand inside the dinosaur to give sermons at times. Wat That Phra Aram Luang temple is a stunning sight to behold on its own, resplendent with numerous golden peaks and facades painted in bright shades or red.

items.body:
# When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery

The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the Vancouver Art Gallery , and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend PaRx , Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access. Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

## An artful approach to treatment

The process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

The prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

After the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

This is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs. The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

Carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She says the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

“For them to understand that so many people have come together to create this opportunity, I think that in and of itself is special,” Fry says. “They say, ‘Wow, my community cares.’ The possibility that this exists, it’s available, it’s free—there’s something about that . . . that’s noteworthy.”

Fry is one of the professionals who gives these kinds of prescriptions to her clients. It’s another tool available to promote well-being.

“Of course, I’m never telling them to go. We talk about this as a prescription, but I always present it as ‘here’s an opportunity to meet some of your goals, and here’s what the opportunity looks like,’” she says.

As yet, no one has declined her prescription.

“They’re surprised that something so seemingly simplistic as slowing down and really looking, really living in front of the art or in nature is actually an intervention,” Fry says. “People in our culture are set up to think that growth has got to be painful, growth has got to be difficult, growth has got to be expensive, growth is going to take a long time. When I bring forward an intervention of going to a location, and your job as a client of mine is to appreciate, the first reaction is surprise. It opens up an entire conversation—‘I can just appreciate my life and not always be grinding to make it better.’ It’s a special process for me to witness.”

## Awe and nature in community

The goal is to do more than increase the number of people who have exposure to art, though that might be a side effect. The formal prescription to nature through art is designed to reduce stress, anxiety, and social isolation. The ability to bring a guest, as well as the opportunity to experience art with other patrons, is key.

items.body:
**Illustration from i went fishing with my family when i was five. Courtesy of Tao Lin.**

I wrote this in February 2005, when I was [twenty-one](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2025/08/05/my-college-diary/):

> i went fishing with my family when i was five
> when i was five
> i went fishing with my family
> my dad caught a turtle
> my mom caught a snapper
> my brother caught a crab
> i caught a whale
> that night we ate crab
> the next night we ate turtle
> the next night we ate snapper
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> …

The first draft repeated the last line 143 times. I sent it to an editor at *Monkeybicycle* —an online literary magazine—and he accepted it for publication. He wrote:

> The average weight of a small sea turtle is 60 lbs. The largest whale (the Blue Whale) averages 120 tons. So, that’s 4000 times larger. I was thinking we could repeat the final line 4000 times.

I emailed the poem to my mom, who replied, “Children would enjoy it very much, what do you think? Maybe sometimes you can write something for children someday. Just have a question, there are several hundred lines of ‘the next night we ate whale,’ is it supposed to be like that or it is a mistake? I tried to delete it, but couldn’t.”

The *Monkeybicycle* editor sent me his 24,059-word file of the poem and suggested I find an illustrator and publish it as “a huge chapbook.” Another *Monkeybicycle* editor said he’d illustrate and lay it out, but I wasn’t interested.

I read the poem at readings maybe five or six times. I remember staying focused and serious while reading it by dwelling on how depressed and alienated I felt. The longest I ever read it was seven minutes, I think.

In 2008, my friend recorded a video of the audience as I read the poem. This video is on YouTube. I began the reading by saying, “I’m going to read from my memoir.” Afterward, I sold stapled booklets of a short version of the poem for three dollars.

In 2009, I was paid a hundred dollars to read the poem for four minutes at the New Museum of Contemporary Art. In 2010, the *London Review of Books* published an [overview](https://www.theparisreview.org/letters-essays/8475/gemstone-tao-lin) of my [writing](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2024/09/12/my-childhood-toy-poodles/) [career](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2023/09/11/jets-and-trash/) that referenced the poem, and someone read the poem at a cultural center in Amsterdam. Also in 2010, at an event at Drawn & Quarterly’s bookstore for my second novel, I pitched the poem as a book to D&Q’s owner. I described this in my novel *Taipei* (2013):

> … the owner of Drawn & Quarterly approached and thanked Paul for coming to Montreal. Paul pitched a children’s book, to be illustrated by a known graphic novelist who’d confirmed interest, based on one of his poems—
> when i was five i went fishing with my family
> when i was five
> i went fishing with my family
> my dad caught a turtle
> my mom caught a snapper
> my brother caught a crab
> i caught a whale
> that night we ate crab
> the next night we ate turtle
> the next night we ate snapper
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> —with each line on its own page and the last line repeated as many times as needed. Maybe a different artist could illustrate each page to create a sort of anthology. As a children’s book, due to the content, it would …

The owner didn’t seem interested.

**Illustration from i went fishing with my family when i was five. Courtesy of Tao Lin.**

In 2012, the Asian American Writer’s Workshop asked me to participate in an event. The organization suggested four things I could do. The first was to read the whale poem. I chose another option. I was tired of reading the poem.

In 2013, I got an email that said, “The Head of English at the University of Exeter just randomly sent everyone on the Poetry module a video of you reading ‘i went fishing with my family when i was five’ as an example of how poetry isn’t dull.”

In 2014, Jeffrey Brown, the author of *Clumsy* (2002), one of my favorite graphic novels, agreed to illustrate my whale poem. An editor at McSweeney’s was interested in it for their children’s-book imprint. But this didn’t result in anything.

BBC Singers ’ composition by Jonathan Packham.

I mostly stopped caring about making the poem into a book. Sometimes people messaged me saying they’d performed it at a reading. A band used it as lyrics for a song. A doctoral student at Oxford used it as the text for a composition that the BBC Singers—a professional chamber choir—performed in a workshop setting.

In 2026, I noticed people discussing my poem on X. Pangram had identified it as 100 percent AI-generated. It was the only false positive discovered in a public challenge offering $4,100 to find one from before 2020 that was longer than 749 words.

This gave my poem more attention than it had ever gotten, encouraging me to make and publish the book myself. I handwrote, illustrated, and designed it over a week. I loved the process.

*From* [i went fishing with my family](https://muumuuhouse.com/whalepoem.html)[when i was five](https://muumuuhouse.com/whalepoem.html) *, published today by Muumuu House.*

*Tao Lin is the author of the novels* Leave Society *and* Taipei *, among other books. His poetry collection* Hawaii Years *is forthcoming from Louria Books. His most recent piece for the Daily was “[Taiwan English](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2026/06/24/taiwan-english/).”*

items.body:
My mother tongue is Thai, but for a long time I couldn’t swear in Thai. That was because the international school I went to banned us from speaking Thai on campus. *No native languages, all the better to improve our English*. It was quite a colonial relationship. I remember the colonial roots of my English every time an American complements my fluency, now that I live in the US.

Because of the school ban my Thai was polite, sweet, but not cool. I had no slang. I could not swear. This changed in the last two years of high school. I did the International Baccalaureate, which then required fifty hours of service from each student in order to graduate with the IB diploma. That seemed like a lot of hours to me! I remember my reluctance to leave the beautiful school campus with its duck ponds and Thai sala and venture into the great unknown of the Klong Toei slums.

I was matched to work in an orphanage of kids with HIV. I squeal for babies and toddlers, and was thrilled. Thailand was early to destigmatize HIV/AIDS. I ended up spending years in this orphanage, holding babies with many wonderful volunteers. What bliss, truly. I learned the carrot dance that the toddlers were obsessed with then; I can still sing it. Then, to my chagrin, I was moved out of the baby and toddler center to be with the adolescents. I think there was some glamour to having an international school student among the older kids. I sensed status in their jostling to speak with me. When the teenagers heard me speak, they fell over themselves laughing. How did I sound like such a child! They taught me to swear. We spoke in slang. In my time in Klong Toei, my Thai finally entered adolescence.

I learned a lot in those fifty hours of volunteer service, which I ended up exceeding. First, service feels wonderful. Maybe in the very beginning it was uncomfortable because of self-consciousness—and who could be more self-conscious than a teenager. But even adolescent me was able to relax the *certainty that everyone was judging her* and enjoy the camaraderie. I brought candy, and we’d walk around in a big pack of teenagers through the slum.

I learned that when the rains come, the slum is first to flood and last to drain; I learned it loses power all the time; I learned that people can be proud of where they’re from even when home is a shack made from corrugated tin. I learned that phad thai is best made on a street-side wok; I learned that Muay Thai keeps kids, especially boys, out of trouble. I learned that no one begs nor steals if they can help it; I learned that people are generally kind and keen for friendship. It was a life-changing year, as it was meant to be.

Reflecting back on that period, I am struck by how effective it was to have a service requirement. We studied economics in IB and learned about purchasing power parity, which is the relative cost of a Big Mac in Cambodia, say, versus the US. But walking those streets, paying for food, looking away as buddies fished coins out of pockets, the cut-open plastic water bottles used to beg, and drains—that was a different education in the cost of living. Knowledge moved from head to heart.

Service can be a force-function to generosity. Some of us are born with access to our tender and generous nature; some of us have quite a crust around the heart. For whatever reasons (the causes and conditions of [karma](https://tricycle.org/buddhism-dharma/#samsara-karma-rebirth)) many of us have learned to armor the heart.

All of us are affected by culture, which is a collective karma. Thailand has a collective culture of generosity. It is startling and real. Don’t worry—there’s a shadow side to Thai culture too. I wrote a whole novel to process it.

The culture of the United States is not what I would call an open and generous one. There seems to be fear around opening the heart. It sounds like: *If I’m generous, someone will take advantage of me.*

It’s probably a well-earned fear. But we cannot begin to walk the path of a [bodhisattva](https://tricycle.org/glossary/bodhisattva/) without *dana*, generosity.

We cannot begin to walk the path of a bodhisattva without *dana*, generosity.

In the temple where I teach, students have asked what you should do if you can’t just produce generosity. What then?

It’s a brave question to voice in a room. This is the answer: Force-function generosity with service. Find a way to log fifty hours of service, and the generosity will be there in your heart by the end of that time.

We remain stuck in spiritual adolescence if we have not had a significant period of service and generosity in our lives. Spiritual adolescence is a preoccupation with comfort and status. It can last our whole life if we let it.

If you are ready to progress to adulthood, I recommend engaging in service. Letting go of individual protectiveness, and feeling the wide river of the heart’s flow is actually a relief. It is freeing in and of itself (though it is not Enlightenment). Push the edges of your comfortable existence and commit significant hours to service. It will widen the aperture of your heart and bring flow again. In Thai the word “kindness” literally means “water of the heart.” My mother tongue is wise. Kindness does flow. It arises naturally, without effort. Giving comes naturally, without effort. When there is flow. If there isn’t flow, we have to poke a hole in the armor of the heart. You poke a hole through service.

If you’ve traveled to developing countries from the US, you might have noticed the baseline generosity of most people. One reason for this is because people from a poor place have had to take responsibility for collective well-being. When you are from a poor country, you *know* that no one is coming to bail you out. Here in the US we might have a fantasy of FEMA or the President or the National Guard coming to people’s aid.

…

items.title: The Funniest Books of 2026, recommended by Sophie Ratcliffe
items.subtitle: Every year, the judges of the Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for Comic Fiction select the funniest novel published in the past twelve months.
items.feedText: In 2026, finalists include a Booker-nominated book about a man in a black bag and a Regency rom-com with a very modern sensibility. Judge, academic and author Sophie Ratcliffe talks us through the six-book shortlist. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
items.body:
# The Funniest Books of 2026

Make Your Own List

### The Best Fiction Books » Humour

## The Funniest Books of 2026

### recommended by Sophie Ratcliffe

Every year, the judges of the Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for Comic Fiction select the funniest novel published in the past twelve months. In 2026, finalists include a Booker-nominated book about a man in a black bag and a Regency rom-com with a very modern sensibility. Judge, academic and author Sophie Ratcliffe talks us through the six-book shortlist.

Interview by Cal Flyn , Deputy Editor

- Read 1 A Good Person by Kirsten King
- Read 2 Black Bag: A Novel by Luke Kennard
- Read 3 How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin
- Read 4 Motherfaker by Anna Brook-Mitchell
- Read 5 Offseason by Avigayl Sharp
- Read 6 We Love You, Bunny: A Novel by Mona Awad
- 1 A Good Person by Kirsten King
- 2 Black Bag: A Novel by Luke Kennard
- 3 How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin
- 4 Motherfaker by Anna Brook-Mitchell
- 5 Offseason by Avigayl Sharp
- 6 We Love You, Bunny: A Novel by Mona Awad
T hank you for talking to us about the six-book shortlist for the 2026 Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for comic fiction. I wonder: is judging humorous writing unusually difficult?

Yes, I think there is a difficulty. I guess what different people find funny or ‘comic’ is pretty subjective. It sounds a touch grave to say that it feels like a responsibility, but it is. We were all trying to come to these books with as open a mind as possible about the varieties of humour that we might encounter. We, as a panel, were looking for books that would make us laugh out loud, but were were also open to those that made us smile or raise an eyebrow, which plunged us into the absurd and grotesque, or the dry and the wry…

Also, crucially, we wanted books that were exceptionally well-written. My own acid test for any really great book – particularly a great comic or joy-giving book – is that I want to press it into the hands of someone who, say, tells me they are going into hospital and need something good to read. Maybe that sounds vague, but these were the rough ingredients of the recipe we were looking for.

A funny book is not the same thing as a light read. They can be both, but a great funny book should still be a quality book.

That’s right. And when I look at the shortlist from this year, that comes through.

Let’s look at those books, one at a time. Can we start with A Good Person by Kirsten King? It features a modern-day hex.

I love this one. Here’s the plot. The heroine of this book breaks up with her boyfriend, who she spent quite a lot of time getting. She also works for a marketing company, and through her work encounters the ‘Wellness Witch’, a social influencer, who gives her the tools to put a ‘hex’ on her ex.

It’s very filmic – King is a screenwriter, and you can tell. I think what stands out in this one is the voice. It’s so good, full of very funny one-liners, which are integrated beautifully. It’s also a page-turner.

The title is A Good Person , and it is very thoughtful about ethics, carried with a light touch. It makes one think about what that means, to be a good person, and what it might be like to want to hex someone, and what to do with shame when things get out of control.

Then all of that is played through a sort of millennial angst about paying rent and having roommates. It’s a gorgeous piece of work: quite dark, very funny.

It’s a classic combination. Comedians are famously troubled. Is there a thread of darkness running through all of the books?

In many of them, yes. There’s quite a lot of trauma and darkness to negotiate in this list. But what the books have in common is that while the dark recesses of the soul might be pondered or traversed, the joke always lands at home. The thread these books have in common is that the comedy is entwined with kindness. They certainly don’t punch down.

Luke Kennard’s Black Bag also featured on the Booker Prize shortlist, which I was delighted to see. I think it’s great. Why did the Wodehouse Prize judges admire it?

Well, it made us all laugh out loud. That’s the first thing. I don’t know if that is the most important thing to say about it, but for this prize it is very important. It’s not a book that is safe to read on a train because you will spill your coffee. And, actually, there’s a fantastic scene involving a coffee mishap—

Yes!

It’s a really, really funny book. So the scenario is based on a real-life psychological experiment where a professor hired someone to wear a large, leather, full-body black bag around the campus of a university to see what happened. So that is clearly completely absurd. The person in this book who is performing as the black bag is a failed actor, and this ‘part’ becomes his starring role. We admired the huge comedy of the novel, but in its construction, Black Bag has really thought through this comic scenario and what it can tell us about what it means to make art, and what it is like to be a human being.

Again, this is a book that does not laugh at anyone, but rather at the predicament of what it means to be human. We also loved the physical comedy. The tiny details. The actor wearing the black bag immacs his lower legs to make sure that no one can work out whether he’s male or female. And he talks brilliantly to the visceral feeling of wearing hot, black leather. There are also interesting themes which emerge around another character who makes a living through livestreams and cryptocurrency. So this book makes us ponder the relationship between the virtual and the material.

It’s a very clever book, but with great humour. You’re physically wincing as you read. It’s masterly.

Well, we have a very different book up next. This is How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin. It’s a Regency rom-com . Tell us more.

…

items.body:
From plates of ravioli and spaghetti to bottles of chianti and sardines springing from their tins, [Kate Jenkins](https://katejenkinsstudio.co.uk/)‘ immersive art-meets-restaurant experience is something to really sink your teeth into. Known for her realistic knitted foodstuffs, the Brighton-based artist and knitwear designer presents *Kate’s Knitalian* at [Air Contemporary](https://www.air-contemporary.com/), inviting us to consider the (rather unexpected) mouthwatering possibilities of yarn.

For the opening reception, visitors were required to reserve a spot much as one would do to book a table in a traditional restaurant, including two timed sittings. Everything from wheels of salami and tortellini to tiramisù and bottles of “Pinot Stitchio” fill the delicatessen experience in a celebration of Italian cuisine.

*Kate’s Knitalian* continues through December 22 in London. And if you find yourself in Brighton, you can visit the artist’s studio, which is open daily in Arundel Place. See more on Jenkins’ [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/kjcardigan). You might also enjoy Lucy Sparrow’s *The Beginning of Convenience,* an entirely [felted supermarket](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/lucy-sparrow-the-beginning-of-convenience/) at The Momentary in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Photo by Helena Dolby

items.body: Background: Mental health conditions are a leading cause of disability and economic burden worldwide. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) may widen access, but economic evidence from community mental health settings, including low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), has not been synthesized by perspective, time horizon, and comparator type. Objective: This study aimed to assess the cost-effectiveness of DMHIs delivered in community mental health settings. Methods: This systematic review followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 guidelines and was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO CRD420251141326). PubMed, Scopus, the Directory of Open Access Journals, and the Cochrane Library were searched for economic evaluations published from January 2010 to June 2025 involving adolescents (aged 10 years and older) through older adults with mental disorders. Two reviewers independently screened studies, and the quality was appraised using the Consensus on Health Economic Criteria (CHEC) list. Costs were standardized to 2025 US $, and findings were synthesized narratively. Results: Of 2478 records identified, 20 economic evaluations were included: 16 randomized controlled trials, 3 decision-analytic models, and 1 uncontrolled single-arm study, conducted in high-income countries and LMICs (Kenya, Lebanon, China, and Southeast Europe). Depression (n=11, 55%) and anxiety (n=7, 35%) were the most frequent targets. Of 20 studies, 10 (50%) used a health care payer perspective only, 1 (5%) study used a societal perspective only, and 9 (45%) used both perspectives; time horizons ranged from 2 weeks to 10 years. Thirteen (65%) studies were cost-effective at the willingness-to-pay thresholds applied, and 4 (20%) were not; 3 (15%) did not state a threshold. Among the 16 studies reporting quality-adjusted life years, 4 (25%) were dominant (less costly and more effective), 11 (69%) were more costly and more effective, and 1 (6%) was less costly and less effective. The BlueIce smartphone app for self-harm and the NIDUS-Family (New Interventions for Independence in Dementia Studies) dementia intervention were dominant, whereas a societal perspective made some interventions cost-saving, such as Step-by-Step in Lebanon. Interventions that were not cost-effective included those evaluated in Germany, the United States, and Southeast Europe, and 1 psychosis trial with a high incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. Methodological quality was high in 15 (75%) studies, moderate in 4 (20%), and low in 1 (5%). Conclusions: DMHIs in community settings can offer good value for money, particularly guided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy for depression and anxiety, and may be cost-saving from a societal perspective. The evidence is limited by short time horizons (often 12 months or less), waitlist and usual care comparators, and heterogeneous outcome measures. Future evaluations should use longer follow-ups, active comparators, and a common utility measure, ideally the EQ-5D questionnaire. Trial Registration: PROSPERO CRD420251141326; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251141326

## The Fall of the House of Usher , The Tell-Tale Heart , and More">25 Films Inspired by Edgar Allan Poe Online: The Fall of the House of Usher , The Tell-Tale Heart , and More

in Film , Literature | November 24th, 2026 Leave a Comment

-->

Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and sev­er­al adap­ta­tions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” will almost cer­tain­ly come near the top. At first glance, that sto­ry of a man pay­ing a vis­it to an old friend who lives with his twin sis­ter in their fam­i­ly’s grand house — each of the lat­ter three well advanced into a dif­fer­ent process of dete­ri­o­ra­tion — might seem too short, as well as too light on con­flict to trans­late into a con­ven­tion­al screen­play. Yet it’s also full of cin­e­mat­i­cal­ly irre­sistible images, from the some­how ruinous yet whol­ly intact tit­u­lar man­sion to the blood­i­ly wretched sis­ter throw­ing her­self upon the ter­ri­fied broth­er who entombed her alive while their ances­tral home col­laps­es around them.

Of the twen­ty or thir­ty ver­sions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” so far made for the screen, the most cel­e­brat­ed remains the one Jean Epstein direct­ed in 1928. Offi­cial­ly des­ig­nat­ing it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that pic­ture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunt­ing spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast mar­ble expanse, inter­rupt­ed here and there by an item of fur­ni­ture that seems dwarfed by the sur­round­ing empti­ness. An odd stair­case ris­es from one dis­tant cor­ner. It is not impos­si­ble that this vision, in one of the best-known French sur­re­al­ist films, inspired the design­ers of the great hall of Xanadu in Cit­i­zen Kane .”

The avant-garde film­mak­ing duo James Sib­ley Wat­son Jr. and Melville Web­ber (in col­lab­o­ra­tion with e. e. cum­mings, who con­tributed to the script) could hard­ly man­age the same scale of pro­duc­tion design for their own short adap­ta­tion of Poe’s sto­ry , which hap­pened to come out the same year.

But the result­ing Expres­sion­ist take on the mate­r­i­al has also been high­ly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films , you can expe­ri­ence not just both of them, but also oth­er adap­ta­tions of “The Fall of the House of Ush­er” by idio­syn­crat­ic Czech ani­ma­tor Jan Švankma­jer and B‑movie pow­er­house Roger Cor­man . Sen­si­tive to Poe’s sen­sa­tion­al­ist appeal and air of trans­gres­sive deca­dence, Cor­man end­ed up direct­ing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” near­ly all of which star Vin­cent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more close­ly asso­ci­at­ed with Poe than Price, a link Tim Bur­ton cel­e­brat­ed in ani­ma­tion at the begin­ning of his career. Price even played the writer him­self in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe , a spe­cial from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amon­til­la­do,” “The Pit and the Pen­du­lum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapt­ed Poe sto­ry of them all, also appears on the playlist in var­i­ous forms: an ear­ly D. W. Grif­fith fea­ture , the direc­to­r­i­al debut of Jules Dassin , an ani­mat­ed short nar­rat­ed by James Mason , a British psy­cho­log­i­cal thriller , and a trans­po­si­tion into mod­ern-day New Orleans . And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watch­ing through all 25 of these films, con­sid­er watch­ing the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Ush­er minis­eries on Net­flix — an enter­tain­ment plat­form that sat­is­fies much the same appetites Poe’s sto­ries have been feed­ing for near­ly two cen­turies.

items.title: Clinical Neurophonetic mechanisms of complex Arabic phoneme articulation: implications for motor and cognitive rehabilitation

items.body: Neurogenic communication disorders, including post-stroke aphasia, dysarthria, and apraxia of speech, remain major challenges in neurological rehabilitation and frequently lead to persistent functional disability. Conventional speech therapy often relies on simplified phonetic targets that may provide limited neuromotor stimulation and insufficient engagement of distributed speech motor networks. The Arabic phonetic system contains several articulatorily complex sounds that require coordinated activation of pharyngeal, uvular, and laryngeal structures, potentially offering a more intensive neuromotor stimulus for rehabilitation. This review synthesizes evidence from neurolinguistics, neuroimaging, clinical speech therapy, and computational speech analysis to examine the therapeutic potential of complex Arabic phonemes—such as Ḍād (/dˤ/), ʿAyn (/ʕ/), and Qāf (/q/)—as targeted exercises for speech recovery. The articulation of these phonemes requires precise coordination of respiratory, laryngeal, and articulatory musculature, engaging distributed cortical and subcortical speech networks. Rather than relying on simplified targets, training with this phonetic complexity stimulates preserved motor pathways and promotes neuroplastic reorganization. Crucially, auditory cortical regions contribute to sensorimotor integration by comparing predicted and actual speech outputs, driving feedforward and feedback-based error correction across cortico-cerebellar and basal ganglia circuits that support adaptive speech recovery. By framing phonetic complexity as a therapeutic resource, this review integrates insights from classical phonetics, neurolinguistics, and contemporary neuroscience to propose a clinically oriented framework for speech rehabilitation. This perspective highlights the translational potential of Arabic phoneme articulation as a model for strengthening motor coordination, supporting neuroplastic adaptation, and advancing culturally informed, technology-assisted strategies for personalized speech therapy across diverse linguistic populations.

items.body:
# XMP OS Offers an Open-Source Alternative Workflow for MPC Live Mk1

Abstract Engineering has released XMP OS , a free, open-source, clip-based music workstation designed initially for the original Akai MPC Live Mk1 .

The project offers an alternative to the standard MPC workflow, with an emphasis on building beats, editing clips, trying variations and launching scenes from the hardware controls.

XMP OS combines tracks, clips and scenes with drum machines, samplers, synthesizers and effects. Its pad-focused workflow is designed to keep common performance and arrangement tasks close at hand, while a browser-based version lets users explore the interface before installing anything on their hardware.

The project is also intended as an extensible development framework. Its public source includes the underlying audio and sequencing systems, hardware-control support, project storage, a shared touchscreen interface, SDK examples and developer documentation. Developers can create instruments and effects, customize interfaces or build new workflows.

The current hardware target is the MPC Live Mk1 with the ACV8 board, running MPC OS 3.10.1. XMP OS boots from a USB drive after a one-time loader setup. The project is currently identified by its developer as a prerelease, and installation support is limited to the stated hardware and firmware configuration. The developer says the Intel Mac installation route has been verified; Apple Silicon laptop testing and Windows physical driver/flash qualification are still pending. The installer applications are also not notarized on macOS and are unsigned on Windows.

Features:

- Clip-based music workstation organized around tracks, clips and scenes
- Drum machines, samplers, synthesizers and effects
- Pad- and hardware-control-focused beatmaking and arrangement workflow
- Browser-based version for trying the workflow without installing the hardware system
- Open-source framework for custom instruments, effects, interfaces and workflows
- SDK, examples, developer documentation and automated test infrastructure
- USB-based startup after a one-time loader installation on the supported MPC Live Mk1 configuration
- Apache 2.0 license for the original XMP code
Pricing & Availability:

XMP OS is free and open source. The browser version, installation downloads, manual and source code are available from Abstract Engineering . The current hardware prerelease is limited to the MPC Live Mk1 / ACV8 running MPC OS 3.10.1; other MPC models are not yet supported for installation.

# 2026 tech gift guide for Apple users — personally tested and recommended - 9to5Mac

## 2026 tech gift guide for Apple users — personally tested and recommended

Black Friday week is here, so it’s officially time to start checking gifts off your list. For my 2026 tech gift guide, I’m recommending technology products that I’ve personally used all year. Each of these products has been especially useful this year, and they’ll make great gifts for the Apple users in your life.

## Apple devices and audio

### 15-inch M5 MacBook Air

$1,199.00 (reg. $1,499.00) for the current M5 model with 16GB of memory and 512GB of storage

I love my 15-inch MacBook Air. It has room for multiple windows without overlapping and is still thin and light enough to carry around. The Sky Blue finish looks great next to my Glacier iPhone 18 Pro, too.

### M5 iPad Pro and Apple Pencil Pro

11-inch M5 iPad Pro (256GB, Wi-Fi) — $1,099.00 (reg. $1,199.00) Apple Pencil Pro — $99.00 (reg. $129.00)

Some weekends I unwind by casually sketching with my iPad Pro and Apple Pencil Pro in Procreate. Other times I get lost in a TV show. The deep blacks on the OLED display really stand out in dark scenes and dark rooms. It’s the nicest screen I own.

### Astropad Rock Paper Pencil 4.0

$39.99 (reg. $49.99) for the 11-inch iPad Pro (M4 and M5) kit

If you’re giving an iPad and Apple Pencil to someone who likes to sketch, I’d add Astropad’s Rock Paper Pencil 4.0 . The matte screen protector gives the Pencil more drag and clings to the display without adhesive, so you can peel it off when you want the glossy screen back. The kit comes with two graphite-style tips for sketching and two smoother ballpoint tips for taking notes.

### AirPods Pro 3

$149.00 (reg. $249.00)

AirPods Pro 3 are the earbuds I use daily. Apple rates them for up to eight hours of listening on a charge with noise cancellation on, and sound quality is unmatched for their size and price.

### Apple Watch Ultra 4

$699.99 (reg. $799.00) for the 49mm Natural Titanium case with the Translucent Gray Ocean Band

Battery life is a big reason I wear an Ultra. Apple rates the Ultra 4 for up to 50 hours of normal use, so I can leave it on overnight to track my sleep. My favorite change this year is the live heart rate complication . It updates every five seconds and fits in one small spot on the watch face, freeing up the whole row I used to give it.

### Beats Pill

$94.95 (reg. $149.95) in Matte Black

The current Beats Pill is my go-to Bluetooth speaker. Beats rates it for up to 24 hours on a charge. Matte Black is the one on sale, and it comes in plenty of other colors.

## CarPlay accessories

### Beats USB-A to USB-C woven cables

$14.00 (reg. $34.99) for two five-foot cables · $18.99 for one

If your car has a USB-A port for wired CarPlay and your iPhone has USB-C, these woven Beats cables connect the two. Plug one in and you get Maps and music on the dashboard while your iPhone charges. The two-pack costs less than a single cable this week.

### CarlinKit and Twelve South wireless CarPlay adapters

CarlinKit Mini Ultra 3 — $35.99 Twelve South AirFly Drive — $31.99 (reg. $39.99)

These are for cars that already have wired CarPlay. Plug either adapter into the USB port you’d normally use for your iPhone and pair it once. After that, CarPlay connects wirelessly when you get in, so your phone can stay in your pocket. The CarlinKit Mini Ultra 3 is one of my favorite stocking stuffers, and Twelve South’s AirFly Drive is $4 less this week.

## AirTag and Find My trackers

### Apple AirTag and Belkin Secure Holder with Key Ring

AirTag (second generation) — $18.00 (reg. $29.00) for one Belkin Secure Holder with Key Ring — $9.99 (reg. $12.95)

I’d give these two together to someone who’s always looking for their keys on the way out the door. If they’re somewhere in the house, you can make the AirTag chime in Find My. A compatible iPhone can also point you toward the keys as you get closer.

### Nomad Tracking Card

$23.20 (reg. $29.00) with Prime, in white

It took losing my wallet twice to convince me to put a tracker in it. Nomad’s Tracking Card fits in a regular card slot, and I can make it ring from Find My. When the card needs a charge, I put it on the same MagSafe charger I use for my iPhone.

## USB-C chargers and power banks

### UGREEN Nexode Pro 200W power bank

$89.99 (reg. $139.99) with Prime, in blue

When my kids’ iPads are running low during use, I grab the UGREEN Nexode Pro power bank . One USB-C cable pulls out of the pack and the other doubles as the carrying strap. It has a capacity of 25,000mAh, which lasts long enough to actually be useful.

### Belkin Qi2 3-in-1 charging stand

$96.76 for the current 15W Qi2 version

The Belkin 3-in-1 stand I recommended last year still lives on my nightstand. At bedtime, my iPhone snaps onto MagSafe, my Apple Watch goes on the puck when I’m not sleep tracking, and my AirPods charge on the pad underneath.

### Magnetic iPhone battery packs from UGREEN, INIU, and Aulumu

UGREEN MagFlow Air — $52.24 (reg. $79.99) with Prime INIU SnapGo Air — $46.74 (reg. $54.99) Aulumu M10 — $71.98 (reg. $89.98) with the Amazon coupon

The UGREEN MagFlow Air is handy on days when I need my iPhone to last longer. It’s a 10,000mAh battery that’s slim enough to leave on my iPhone when I slip it into my pocket.

If your iPhone supports 25W wireless charging, I’d go with the INIU SnapGo Air. It also holds 10,000mAh and costs the least of the three.

For an overnight trip, I’d bring the Aulumu M10 . My iPhone snaps onto one side, and the Apple Watch charging puck on the back means I can leave my watch cable at home.

## AKAI MPC Sample Update 1.4

Vor ein paar Wochen hatte AKAI angekündigt, die **MPC Sample**für Entwickler zu öffnen (siehe unten). Zeitgleich mit der neuen Firmware 1.4 veröffentlicht der Hersteller nun ein**SDK** (Software Development Kit), mit dem du deine eigenen Effekte entwickeln kannst. Diese tauchen dann in der Liste der Knob FX des Samplers auf und lassen sich wie die mitgelieferten Effekte einsetzen.

Bisher unterstützt das SDK nur die Effekte; um zum Beispiel eigene Synthesizer für die MPC Sample zu erstellen, musst du also weiterhin tiefer in das Thema Firmware-Hacks einsteigen – auf eigene Gefahr. Trotzdem ist es natürlich eine tolle Nachricht, dass AKAI mit der Zeit geht und eigene Entwicklungen auf der Hardware-Plattform ausdrücklich unterstützt.

Darüber hinaus enthält das Update weitere interessante Neuerungen. Mit der neuen Funktion *Resample Pad* kannst du ein Pad mitsamt den dazugehörigen Knob FX in ein neues Sample verwandeln. Auch werden neu aufgenommene Samples, die sich über die gesamte Länge einer Sequenz erstrecken, nun sofort nach Ende der Aufnahme abgespielt. De facto verhält sich die MPC Sample damit also wie ein Looper.

Ebenfalls neu ist der Modus *16 Level Tune (Scale)*. Damit kannst du Samples auf den Pads mit den Noten einer ausgewählten Tonleiter spielen. Den schon bisher verfügbaren chromatischen Modus gibt es natürlich weiterhin.

Das Firmware-Update 1.4 für die MPC Sample steht jetzt auf der Website des Herstellers zum Download bereit.

Die MPC Sample bekommst du bei [Thomann](https://www.thomann.de/de/akai_professional_mpc_sample_bag_bundle.htm?offid=1&affid=84)* – noch bis zum **30.11.2026** im Bundle mit einer passenden Tasche zum Preis, den der Sampler normalerweise ohne Tasche kostet!

## AKAI MPC Sample wird Open Source – und man kann DOOM darauf zocken!

*[29. Oktober 2026]* **Nach der Ankündigung der Sample Key lag es in der Luft: Auch die Firmware der MPC Sample wird im Rahmen einer Open-Source-Lizenz veröffentlicht. Und ja, auch DOOM wurde schon zum Laufen gebracht.**

Gestern überraschte AKAI Professional mit der [Sample Key](https://www.gearnews.de/akai-sample-key-synthesizer/) – einer kleinen Tastaturversion der MPC Sample. Was jedoch noch überraschender war: Die Firmware ist **Open Source**, darf also von jedem modifiziert werden. Damit trägt AKAI dem Trend zu**Vibe-Coding-Hacks** Rechnung.

Im selben Demo-Reel zur Sample Key bestätigt der Hersteller außerdem, dass auch die **MPC Sample**ohne Tastatur die**Open-Source-Firmware**bekommen wird. Unter anderem ist zu sehen, wie ein**Wavetable-Synthesizer**und ein**Chiptune-Synth** darauf laufen. Das verspricht ganz neue klangliche Möglichkeiten für den kleinen Sampler – wir sind gespannt, was der Community so einfällt!

Und auch die wichtigste Frage wurde schon geklärt: Ja, auf der MPC Sample kann man DOOM zocken! Wie man da noch zum Musikmachen kommen soll? Keine Ahnung!

items.body:
## Design Miami 2026 Preview: “Unveiling” Works From 75 International Galleries at This Year’s Miami Art Week

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/design-miami-2026-preview/)

Brodin, “Constellation of Memory,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Kelley and Gavin Brodin.)

[Design Miami](https://designmiami.com/fair/miami-2026), one of the most exciting events of Miami Art Week, is back for the 22nd edition of its flagship fair. The event, devoted to contemporary collectible design, returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with a lineup of 75 international galleries, museum-quality presentations, and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.

The theme, *Unveiling*, calls for the viewers to truly observe each object, deciphering what inspired the artist to create them, and the surrounding stories behind their choices. These may be hiding in plain sight or several times removed from the final result, reflecting something deeply personal or rooted in the artist’s culture. *Unveiling* is then divided among four curatorial threads, each with different approaches and best represented by certain artists, techniques, and galleries.

## Design Miami is back with with a lineup of 75 international galleries and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.

Pippin Drysdale, “Sacred Lands,” 2026. Adrian Sassoon at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Adrian Sassoon, London; photography by Robert Frith, Acorn Photo.)

First up is *Process as Aesthetic: Unveiling the Hand of the Maker*. This theme highlights the creative process, particularly the techniques, labor, and experimentation that come to determine an object’s aesthetic, regarding these steps as a vehicle for expression. This can be seen in the ceramic works of Bouke de Vries and Pippin Drysdale; Caroline Desile’s architecture-influenced *Totem 1*; Richard Haining’s *STACKED* creations, made up of thousands of pieces of salvaged New York City wood; and Man Ray’s *Optic-Topic mask*, the centerpiece of this division.

Le Corbusier, “La licorne passe sur la mer,” 1959. Boccara Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Boccara Gallery.)

Meanwhile, *Subverting Archetypes: The Familiar, Reimagined*, takes a more surrealist route, blurring the line between the familiar and the uncanny, asking viewers to reassess to what they think they know. Such is the case of a selection of 20th-century tapestries by Le Corbusier, Sonia Delaunay, and Alexander Calder. This section also features the work of Brazilian designer Lucas Recchia, who blends metal with fused glass, and a wall piece by Jaydan Moore, who turns found, silver-plated tableware into sculptural forms.

Dee Clements, “Gams,” 2026. Mindy Solomon Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: Clare Britt, courtesy of the artist and Mindy Solomon Gallery)

Prateek Jain & Gautam Seth, “Enchanted Forest,” 2025. Klove Studio at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of klove.)

Glover, “A Natural History of Dreams,” 2022. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Duane Reed Gallery.)

*Material poetry: Unveiling material potential* explores the expectations materials carry, alongside their emotional, sensory, and imaginative possibilities. This is best represented by the work of Dutch designer Frederik Molenschot and Franco-Swedish designer Ingrid Donat, with the former approaching bronze as heavy and imposing, and the latter as luminous and weightless. Fernando Mastrangelo also touches on this with a monolithic sculpture cast from glass and sand that conceals an expandable cabinet within its architectural form.

KAMEH by Nikita Erokhin, “Beyond Reflection,” 2026. KAMEH at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Nikita Berezhnoy.)

Cure, “Color in Suspension,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Laura Hernandez.)

Barford, Light Sculpture “Feast,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of David Gill Gallery)

Finally, *Mirrors of Society and Place: Unveiling Identity, Culture, and Locality* assesses how design can convey identity, values, culture, and collective memory. After all, objects can become reflections of the societies and environments from which they emerge. For this, the fair presents a selection of mid-century Brazilian design, including works by Joaquim Tenreiro, Jorge Zalszupin, and José Zanine Caldas, while also looking their influence on contemporary creatives. Meanwhile, African artists Amber Cowan, Donté Hayes, hettler.tüllmann, Nobuhito Nishigawara, Simphiwe Mbunyuza, and Virginia Leonard Samburu present pieces inspired by Kenya’s landscapes and architecture.

Yakusha, “DOLONIA Sofa,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Victoria Yakusha Gallery.)

Turco, Installation View, 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Alex Turco.)

Design Miami will run on Dec. 1–6. Members, Collectors, and Press Previews will take place on Dec. 1, with a VIP Preview on the morning of Dec. 2. Public Show Days start on Dec. 2 at 1 p.m. To plan your visit and get tickets, visit [Design Miami’s website](https://designmiami.com/fair/miami-2026). To stay up to date, follow [Design Miami on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/designmiami).

items.body:
# Trump suggests Jensen Huang could have moved to China if not reinstated as Nvidia CEO: ‘Got a little blood there’

WASHINGTON — President Trump claimed Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could have become a leader in China’s artificial intelligence industry if he hadn’t been reinstated to the US firm — telling CNBC in a phone interview that the 63-year-old has “got a little blood there” despite being born in Taiwan.

“If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ’Hey, how would you like to come to China?’ — He’s got a little [Chinese] blood in him. He’s got a little blood there — ‘How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei?’” Trump told CNBC in a phone interview, during which he called Huang, 63, a “national treasure” despite his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he could do that.”

Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to restore the AI pioneer 11 days after he resigned — saying he gave the directors assurances that Huang wouldn’t face legal issues over his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation).

If Alice Huang or her Singapore-based Megaspeed firm violated US export laws by sending advanced Nvidia chips to China, “that wouldn’t be Jensen’s fault,” Trump argued.

The president, who returned late Thursday from a trip to China that included a trilateral summit with his counterpart Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, reiterated that “Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you they would give him whatever he wanted.

“And then they’d automatically have you know all of the things. He never even suggested that. But I know how good China is, how professional they are, how cunning they are.”

Trump said during his nearly hour-long interview that he didn’t ask Xi if Alice Huang was a spy — a claim Beijing has denied though Megaspeed was under investigation by Singapore’s government and the US Commerce Department for allegedly flouting US export restrictions on AI chip shipping to China.

“You know, he’s in a class by himself. We would have lost him,” Trump said of Huang, who was sent to the US by his parents at age 9, cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into one of the world’s most valuable companies .

“If I were President Xi, I’d say, ‘Hey, let’s get him over here real fast. He can have whatever he wants. We’ll give him Beijing. Okay, we’ll give him all of Beijing.’”

“Crazy things like that happen,” Trump said.

“I think he’s going to start off at an almost higher level. He’s apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate…. That’s what brought it to such a level because sex sells, fellas.”

von Carsten Knobloch 24. Nov. 2026 | 0

# Image-Line FL Studio 2026: neuer FLEX, verbesserte KI und vieles mehr

## Image-Line FL Studio 2026.2 Digital Audio Workstation

## Release Candidate ist da - was bietet FL Studio 2026.2?

Image-Line FL Studio 2026.2 Digital Audio Workstation

Mit Image-Line FL Studio 2026 hat die belgische Software-Firma im Sommer eine neue Version ihrer DAW herausgebracht. Nun steht der nächste „Release Candidate“ in den Startlöchern, sodass zeitnah FL Studio 2026.2 erscheinen wird – mit erweitertem Stem-Separation-Modell, einem flexibleren Mixer und neuen kreativen Werkzeugen.

## Image-Line FL Studio 2026.2

Image-Line hat am 21. November 2026 den Release Candidate von FL Studio 2026.2 vorgestellt. Das kommende Update bringt zahlreiche Neuerungen für Produzenten und Musiker mit sich.

Ein besonderes Highlight ist die erweiterte Stem-Separation: Das neue 6-Stem-Modell der All-Plug-ins-Edition kann neben den bisherigen Elementen nun auch Gitarren und Klaviere separat extrahieren. Gleichzeitig wurde das 4-Stem-Modell hinsichtlich Geschwindigkeit und Speicherverbrauch optimiert. Davon sollen vor allem Nutzer älterer Computersysteme profitieren.

Stem-Separation in der aktuellen Version 2026

Auch bei der Bedienung legen die Entwickler nach. Shortcuts für Toolbar, Hauptmenü und Channel Rack lassen sich nun individueller konfigurieren und mit dem neuen Nebula Picker kommt zudem eine visuelle Preset-Suche hinzu. Instrumenten-Sounds werden hier als farbige Punkte dargestellt und nach Klangähnlichkeit sowie Genre angeordnet. Das soll die Suche nach passenden Sounds deutlich intuitiver machen.

Weitere Verbesserungen betreffen die Pattern-Verwaltung, MIDI-Funktionen und die Piano Roll. Besonders für die Bereiche Mixing und Mastering interessant ist die Tatsache, dass die Anzahl der Mixer-Effekt-Slots von bisher zehn auf bis zu 25 pro Kanal steigt. Auch das MIDI-Scripting erhält neue Funktionen, darunter Note Repeat und die Unterstützung von Gamepads als Eingabegeräte.

Bei den neuen Plug-ins erweitert Image-Line das Angebot um PitchHiker und Pressure. PitchHiker bietet Echtzeit-Pitchkorrektur, Formantkontrolle, Vibrato und Harmoniefunktionen für Vocals und monophone Instrumente. Pressure ist ein Stereo-Mastering-Kompressor mit elf Kompressionsalgorithmen und verschiedenen Sidechain-Architekturen.

Abgerundet wird das Update durch zahlreiche Plug-in-Optimierungen, GPU-Beschleunigung für Edisons Deverb und Declipper sowie überarbeitete Oberflächen von Morphine und Soundgoodizer.

Wann genau FL Studio 2026.2 final erscheint, ist bisher noch nicht bekannt. Für bestehende Nutzer ist das Update kostenlos. Weitere Infos zum Image-Line FL Studio 2026 findet ihr auf der Produktseite von Image-Line .

## MACHINED ALUMINUM STREET FURNITURE REGULATES URBAN CIRCULATION

Founded in 2026 as a family-run practice working across industrial design, urban planning, and architecture, Terminal Design has introduced a collection of **[street furniture](https://www.designboom.com/tag/street-furniture/)**engineered to regulate circulation and occupation in public spaces. Developed in collaboration with civic partners and refined through full-scale prototype testing, the line encompasses slatted**[benches](https://www.designboom.com/tag/chair-design/)**, staggered lean bars, barriers, and cantilevered shelters produced in limited runs for municipal plazas, corporate courtyards, commercial streets, and transit hubs. Each component is proportioned around calculated inclines, intervals, and facets that support brief stops while discouraging prolonged lounging, maintaining pedestrian flow in congested zones.

calm bench in orange | all images [©Terminal Design Solutions](https://www.terminaldesignsolutions.com)

## BRUSHED GRAIN AND RED, PINK, AND VIOLET tones form CIVIC COLLECTION

Fabricated from machined aluminum with a directional brushed grain and finished in anodized tones of red, pink, and deep violet, the pieces pair orthogonal geometry with weather-resistant durability. Beyond visual contrast, **[the studio](https://www.terminaldesignsolutions.com)** utilizes the thermal conductivity of uninsulated aluminum as a passive behavioral mechanism: by absorbing and radiating seasonal heat in summer and cold in winter, the metal surfaces naturally limit seating duration without active enforcement.
