items.body:
# What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?

Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis . The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

## Tackling Riemann

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”

The proof of the hypothesis was announced by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.

But it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.

The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.

## Proof factories

It’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.

But AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.

When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.

AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.

The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.

## Deriving worries

Mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter . We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.

Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.

But that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever issues they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.

Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce new insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.

How mathematicians are expected to identify new challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.

items.title: A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space
items.subtitle: Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) stars spread heavy elements into space with their stellar winds.
items.feedText: This material eventually forms more stars, and even rocky planets like ours. For a long time, astronomers thought this important mass-loss was driven by stellar winds. But new research shows how magnetic fields play an important role. A vast flare and magnetic loop of material from the AGB star Mira provides the evidence.
items.body:
# A Gigantic Stellar Eruption Spreads Planetary Material Into Space

Highly-evolved stars spread the material for new planets and stars into space with their stellar winds. These stars are called aysmptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, and they're cool, luminous stars that are running out of hydrogen and leaving the main sequence behind. As they age, they can shed as much as 30 Earth masses of material per year into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The material is first emitted in pulses of gas, and eventually that gas cools into dust and the star's radiation pressure pushes it away with its stellar wind. Carbon and silica are important parts of what's emitted, and silica is the main building block for rocky planets, while carbon feeds into organic particles. So these stellar winds from AGB stars clearly play an important role in the formation of planets, other stars, and even potential life.

Researchers at Chalmers University in Sweden have been observing Mira, an AGB star about 300 light years away. It's the prototype and namesake of what are called Mira variables, pulsating AGB stars that are oxygen-rich. Their results are challenging the long-held understanding that stellar winds driven by radiation pressure are what spread heavy elements into the interstellar medium (ISM).

The research is " A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic-giant-branch star Mira A ," and it's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics. The lead author is Wouter Vlemmings, Professor in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, Sweden.

"Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained," the authors write. "This mass-loss process is crucial for the chemical enrichment of the Universe."

Since this type of mass-loss is so fundamental, it's attracted a lot of attention and is the subject of a huge amount of research. In this work, the researchers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observations to study how Mira's magnetic fields might shape its mass loss. ALMA can't directly observe magnetic fields; instead it observes them indirectly through their polarizing effect on radio emissions.

“For decades, astronomers have believed that the winds from stars like this must be powered by starlight. Light from the star shines on grains of dust in the star’s outer atmosphere, and that gives them a push. But this star is showing us something different: that strong magnetic fields can also shape and power stellar winds. That changes a fundamental part of the origin story of the atoms we ourselves are made of," lead author Vlemmings explained in a press release .

This schematic shows the structure of an AGB star, from its degenerate core to its circumstellar envelope. It shows it during its thermal pulse stage, when pulses drive gas outward, where it cools and forms dust in the envelope. Radiation pressure generates the stellar wind that drives the dust away into the ISM. Image Credit: Lu et al. Front. Astron. Space Sci., 23 July 2025. Sec. Astrostatistics

Astrophysicists have detected strong magnetic fields in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars like Mira, and researchers have suggested that they may play a role in driving their mass loss. But the researchers explain that there's been no empirical evidence of the role magnetic fields play in the process, and that wind-driven mass loss models don't include magnetic fields.

Recent observations, however, are challenging the overall understanding of the wind-driven mass loss scenario. Some AGB stars show mass-loss but also show insufficient dust to explain it. These stars are oxygen-rich AGB stars like Mira. Since Mira is the nearest of its type of dusty, pulsation-driven O-rich AGB stars, it makes sense to study it.

Both ALMA and the Very Large Array recently observed Mira A, the AGB star, and its companion Mira B, a white dwarf, in August 2025. But observations go back ten years, and both sets of data combine to reveal dramatic changes on Mira A's surface.

"During the past decade, high-angular-resolution observations of Mira A at visible, millimetre, and submillimetre wavelengths have revealed several unexpected phenomena related to the stellar atmosphere and mass-loss process," the authors write.

This ten-year study of Mira's surface is the longest study of any star other than the Sun.

This time-lapse shows ten years of changes on the surface of Mira A. Credit: W. Vlemmings et al. 2026. Astronomy and Astrophysics.

“We were astonished to see how the star’s surface is constantly changing. The brightest areas were different every time we looked, and the brightest patches are amazingly bright. We realised that star is flaring, releasing vast amounts of energy each time," said study co-author Miora Andriantsaralaza, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of Physics and Astronomy at Chalmers University of Technology.

Some of the hotspots in the video have brightness temperatures of 8,000 Kelvin. That's far higher than the average 2,000 K brightness temperature.

But the main finding is what researchers call SiO (silicon monoxide) masers. They're often found in the circumstellar envelopes of AGB stars, just inside the dust formation zone. But Mira A's masers are at a much greater distance, where the gas is too thin for a strong SiO maser to form. So the researchers say the masers trace a shock moving outward, and that it has much higher density than expected. In short, a flare that expanded into a huge loop of expelled material.

items.body:
Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.

The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with [1,638 cases as of November 23](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles). Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.

## Deaths and transmission

On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its [third measles death](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/news/releases/112426.htm), an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, [an infant](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/news/releases/110526.htm) and [a child](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/news/releases/111326.htm). New York has also reported a [death, which was of a 7-month-old baby](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/36693/AAP-president-Child-s-death-in-New-York-another?autologincheck=redirected). On November 20, Virginia reported the death of [a child between the age of 0 and 4](https://www.vdh.virginia.gov/news/public-relations-contacts/2026-news-releases/vdh-1st-measles-death-2026/).

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/11/measles-death-toll-rises-to-14-as-national-case-tally-nears-6000/)

items.title: Does It Really Matter If There’s an Intelligence Explosion?
items.subtitle:
Noah Smith at Noahpinion:

“Pacing the frontier” so that alignment research can catch up might be effective in a world of steady linear AI progress.
items.feedText: But in a world of sudden superexponential progress, AI alignment research will immediately be left behind. Even if there is a Singularity for understanding alignment, in a world with an intelligence explosion it will be the superintelligent AI, not us, that carries out that Singularity and decides on its alignment for itself. items.body:
Noah Smith at *Noahpinion*:

“Pacing the frontier” so that alignment research can catch up might be effective in a world of steady linear AI progress. But in a world of sudden superexponential progress, AI alignment research will immediately be left behind. Even if there is a Singularity for understanding alignment, in a world with an intelligence explosion it will be the superintelligent AI, not us, that carries out that Singularity and decides on its alignment for itself.

A second point is that it’s not obvious why an intelligence explosion would be more dangerous than — or even distinguishable from — the type of rapid, non-explosive progress we’re already getting. Remember, AI going from “can’t add two numbers together” to “solves problems too hard for all human mathematicians combined” in three years is *not* counted as an intelligence explosion!

It’s clear that at the current rate of steady progress, AI will become superhuman in most domains in a fairly small number of years. Even robotics and other physical tasks [look conquerable](https://www.understandingrobots.org/p/openais-astra-model-is-shockingly) with the current type of AI that powers Claude and GPT. This means that AI will basically look like a god within our lifetimes, *whether or not* it looks like the kind of infinitely self-improving gods that populate Vernor Vinge novels.

This is why I’m not sure what an intelligence explosion means for our economy. It’s [easy to write down a model](https://aleximas.substack.com/p/will-ai-soon-lead-to-double-digit) in which smoothly increasing AI capabilities drive a smooth increase in GDP. But why should we believe a model like that?

More [↗ noahpinion.blog](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/does-it-really-matter-if-theres-an).

# Skipper, Tripod, and finding apps that fit

- Skipper, Tripod, and finding apps that fit – Six Colors MENU This Week's Sponsor Magic Lasso Adblock : Block ads in iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple TV apps By Jason Snell November 24, 2026 12:00 PM PT ■ apps Skipper, Tripod, and finding apps that fit We live in a world with so many monolithic apps and services, dominated by giant companies. So one of my favorite things is to explore little software niches that haven’t been captured by the major players. Instead of one or two pretty samey apps, you can end up with a whole forest of wild variations on the theme, each fueled by developers making specific choices about how to present information and serve users. When I compare these apps, I realize that there’s really no right or wrong—there are just choices, some of which might work for me, some of which won’t. I’m not offended when an app isn’t made for me, but I can be delighted when an app does slide perfectly into my life. After a year of using Television Time (not to be confused with the now-defunct TV Time ) to log my TV viewing and (more importantly) let me keep track of what we’re watching next and what we’d like to get to next, I discovered an app that just served me better. That’s Skipper , Yoav Zoldan’s new app, available for $30/year or $3/month. What sold me on it is that its primary screen is a list of shows I’m watching with the next episode marked, sorted in a way that makes sense to me. I only want to interact with the app in a handful of ways: seeing what to watch next, checking the box indicating that we watched it, and occasionally searching to add a show that I might be interested in watching next. Television Time required more swiping around and entering detail views, and one thing I’ve discovered about myself is that I prefer apps that are optimized to present all the information I want in one place, and which limit the number of swipes and taps required to navigate around. Skipper hit that sweet spot for me—your mileage, of course, may vary. Skipper has a lot of other features, including a very clever one that compares your watch list to your streaming service subscriptions and can nudge you to drop that service you’re not actually using, complete with a calendar of when shows you watch will be returning. (I know, I know, I shouldn’t have subscribed to BritBox. I have no time to watch it!) It’s not entirely accurate—it doesn’t seem to understand that I watch sports on YouTube TV and things that are not shows on YouTube Premium—but it’s a smart feature that could help a lot of people who are not inveterate streaming subscription sickos like me. Just as there are many TV-tracking apps, there are many, many podcast apps. I’ve been using Overcast for ages , and it just fits into how I want to listen to podcasts. I spend as little time as possible picking what to listen to (there’s my optimization streak again) and have Overcast configured to give me that. But there have been other podcast apps that serve other, equally valid, points of view. Castro really made its name by not just offering a beautiful interface, but a clever “triage” system that brings new episodes into an inbox. Then the user manually decides what’s worth adding to the play queue. Clearly that approach clicked with a lot of people, making Castro a fan favorite even through its ongoing business challenges and different owners . Which brings me to an impressive new podcast app that’s been designed to appeal especially to Castro fans: Ben Rice McCarthy’s Tripod . Ben is a really talented designer, and the app looks gorgeous and works well. It’s built around the same Inbox concept as Castro, so Castro users will feel right at home. I got to beta test Ben’s app for a while, and was incredibly impressed—especially at how it works on the iPhone Duo. That all said, I am just not the target audience for Tripod—and that’s okay. The way Overcast works for podcasts is the way I want to work. Quite frankly, the idea of having another Inbox to check does not fill my heart with joy, even if the podcasts found therein would bring me that joy. That’s on me, not on Ben, and not on Tripod. So if you watch TV like me, you should try Skipper . And if you’re not like me, you should try Tripod . That’s the beauty of these app niches; they don’t have to be all things to all people, they just need to find their audience and serve them well. Report a typo

Explore This Section

- [Science](https://science.nasa.gov/)
- [Citizen Science](https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/)
- Amateur Astronomer? Be a…
- [Overview](https://science.nasa.gov/learn)
- [Resources](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/resources)
- [Opportunities](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/learner-opportunities/)
- [Citizen Science](https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/)
- [Highlights](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/science-activation-highlights)
- [About Science Activation](https://science.nasa.gov/learn/about-science-activation/)

Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a [kilonova](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/glossary/#kilonova). These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s [Kilonova Catcher](https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/kilonova-catcher/?utm_medium=nasa-science&utm_source=summary-page&utm_campaign=launch-highlight) project!

Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network. When [gravitational wave](https://science.nasa.gov/universe/glossary/#gravitational-waves) detectors or space telescopes send out an alert, volunteers point their own telescopes at the sky to help find and track the fading light. The network also follows up on gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the universe, and catches other short-lived cosmic events whenever the opportunity arises.

The Kilonova Catcher network has more than 150 registered members on several continents. Volunteers work side by side with professional astronomers and observatories. They have already contributed to more than 64 official reports shared through NASA’s General Coordinates Network, the system scientists use to share discoveries in real time. Volunteers’ observations have been credited for their contributions by being named authors in peer-reviewed scientific research papers. Kilonova Catcher volunteers also joined NASA’s lunar [Impact Flash!](https://science.nasa.gov/citizen-science/impact-flash/) project campaign during the Artemis II mission, recording the tiny flashes of light made when meteoroids strike the Moon. The network is getting ready to help follow up thousands of new alerts from NASA’s new [Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/).

“Here at Kilonova Catcher, by chasing the light from gravitational-wave events, we’re seeing how a single collision reaches across the universe,” said Cristina Andrade, Kilonova Catcher head of operations at the Minnesota Institute for Astrophysics. “The observatories that make this possible will produce an unprecedented amount of data. We need more human minds, more people with their eyes on the sky and on the data, both literally and figuratively. And more importantly, we need more people to realize they are capable of great feats of science, regardless of their background.”

The Kilonova Catcher project is co-led by Andrade and Principal Investigator Dr. Damien Turpin, a researcher at the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA). Damien said, “I am inspired by the expertise and drive of our amateur astronomers. They are always digging for more information and pushing the limits of their understanding. This science could not be done without their contributions.”

To register and become a Kilonova Catcher, visit [https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/](https://kilonovacatcher.in2p3.fr/) or send an email to kilonovacatcher@gmail.com. Anyone who has access to a telescope with a camera can take part!

On Aug. 17, 2017, the[Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory](https://www.ligo.caltech.edu/) (LIGO) and the[Virgo Interferometer](https://www.ego-gw.it/public/about/whatIs.aspx) both detected gravitational waves from the collision between two neutron stars. Within 12 hours observatories had identified the source of the event within the lenticular galaxy NGC 4993, shown in this image, which was gathered with NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope. The associated kilonova is clearly visible in the Hubble observations. This is the first time the optical counterpart of a gravitational wave event was observed. Hubble observed the kilonova gradually fading over the course of six days, as illustrated by the three time-stamped inset images made between Aug. 22 and 28.

## Learn More and Get Involved

## Kilonova Catcher

Use your backyard telescope to spot the most cataclysmic collisions in our Universe!

items.body:
NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft.

The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.

NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will launch on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket to deliver research and supplies to the International Space Station.

NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will deliver approximately 11,000 pounds of research and supplies to the International Space Station.

NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Mission 25 will launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 spacecraft is named in honor of NASA astronaut James “Jim” A. Lovell Jr. Lovell flew four missions, including Gemini VII, Gemini XII, Apollo 8, and the Apollo 13 mission around the Moon.

NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney will be on duty during the Cygnus spacecraft’s approach and rendezvous. Watkins will be at the controls of the Canadarm2 robotic arm, ready to capture Cygnus as Delaney monitors the spacecraft’s arrival.

## Science highlights

In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments aimed at improving drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis treatment, predicting cancer spread, advancing treatments for muscle loss, improving radiation sensing, and supporting food production for future long-duration missions. This research includes:

### Cardinal Muscle 2.0

Preflight image of the Biocell bioreactor system used to maintain engineered muscle tissue samples as part of the Advancing Therapeutic Treatment of Sarcopenia (Cardinal Muscle 2.0) investigation. Aboard the International Space Station, this investigation tests the effects of potential therapeutics on human muscle cell cultures. The research may help accelerate development of treatments for age-related muscle loss on Earth and support astronaut health during long-duration missions.

[Cardinal Muscle 2.0](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/station/research-explorer/investigation/?#id=9031) uses the microgravity environment to explore potential treatments for muscle loss. Muscle atrophy and strength loss experienced by astronauts after spaceflight share many features with age-related muscle decline on Earth and occur more rapidly in microgravity without exercise. Researchers will use a muscle tissue model to test different Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs used to treat other conditions can be repurposed to prevent or reduce muscle loss.

### DNA NANO B

A confocal microscope image shows a human cartilage cell, with its nucleus stained in blue, following delivery of Janus Base Nanoparticles (JBNp) and the subsequent release of bioactive mRNA (pink) that was translated into function protein (green). Biomimetic Fabrication of Multi-Functional DNA-Inspired Nanomaterials via Controlled Self-assembly in Space (DNA Nano Therapeutics-Mission 2) continues prior research on in-space manufacturing of nanomaterials that mimic DNA and have applications for vaccines and regenerative medicine.

The [DNA Nano B](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/station/research-explorer/investigation/?#id=9654) investigation uses microgravity to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles designed to deliver medicine into dense tissues, such as cartilage and solid tumors. Microgravity may enable more uniform particle assembly, helping researchers refine production methods. The results could advance targeted treatments for cancer and osteoarthritis on Earth.

### ARES

Preflight image of an Active Radiation Environment Sensor (ARES) unit undergoing ground testing in a thermal vacuum chamber. This investigation monitors radiation in habitable spacecraft environments and has exposure awareness and warning capabilities for Human Landing System crews. Testing aboard the International Space Station helps researchers validate the technology for future exploration missions.

The Active Radiation Environment Sensor ([ARES](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/station/research-explorer/investigation/?#id=9537)) will test a small radiation monitoring device to support future Artemis program and lunar missions. The system is designed to integrate with spacecraft systems and provide real-time radiation monitoring inside crew living areas. The results could inform radiation monitoring strategies and crew safety measures for future exploration missions.

### ENCAPSULATE-1

Preflight image of colorectal microtumors grown within Encapsulate’s biochip. The investigation, Encapsulate nVasive: Unraveling the Enigma of Metastasis – Flight 1, or Encapsulate-1, grows copies of patients’ tumor samples aboard the International Space Station to study how cancer cells move and interact in microgravity. Results may help researchers develop further testing to predict a patient’s risk of metastasis and support more personalized cancer treatments.

[Encapsulate-1](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/station/research-explorer/investigation/?#id=9594) uses miniature replicas of patients’ tumors to study how cancer cells move, invade surrounding tissues, and potentially spread. Researchers aim to develop a space-based diagnostic tool that could predict cancer progression months or even years in advance, improving early detection and treatment decisions for patients on Earth.
